title: Where a vLLM cold start goes
question: Where does a cold [vLLM](p1:vllm) start on a rented GPU spend its time, and which empty cache is worth warming more: the weights or the [compiled GPU code](p1:compile)? One also bought serving memory ([KV cache](p1:kvcache)).

requirements.text: Split one [cold start](p1:coldstart) into named phases, and label time that cannot be attributed instead of hiding it.
requirements.why: The caches act on different phases ([weights](p1:weights) on loading, [compile](p1:compile) on engine start), so one "startup" bar would hide half the experiment.

requirements.text: Any two set-ups compared differ only in cache configuration: same image, entrypoint and engine flags.
requirements.why: Otherwise a difference cannot be pinned on a cache.

requirements.text: Report each arm's spread as percentiles, and give every comparison its own interval.
requirements.why: Cold starts are skewed with a heavy tail, so a mean describes no real run. "Cache X matters more" needs its own interval, not two point estimates side by side.

requirements.text: Commit the hypotheses, which runs get thrown out, when to stop and how the headline is chosen, before the first campaign run (three paid reconnaissance captures came first).
requirements.why: Git timestamps then show the rules came before the campaign data, and the headline cannot be picked by which result cost the most effort.

requirements.text: Run on paid GPUs only code already tested offline, and let anyone re-derive every number on a laptop.
requirements.why: The whole budget was $200, and debugging on live GPUs eats it. A number a reader cannot re-derive must be taken on trust.
requirements.unlinked_reason: It is met by process: the flow's "Build against the captures; test it end to end" tests the code on recorded logs and a free fake engine, and "Analyse from the committed store" re-derives every number with no GPU.

concepts.plain: Three cache set-ups. **A**: weights from the model hub, [compile cache](p1:compile) cold. **B**: weights from a network volume, compile cache cold. **C**: weights from the volume, compile cache warm.
One run of each arm, in an order shuffled from a seed. 100 triples make the 300 runs, so a busy hour on the rented GPUs falls on all three arms.

A **contrast** is the difference of two arms' medians, with a 95% [bootstrap interval](p2:interval), a plausible range for the true difference, not where a re-run would land: A minus B is the weight cache's saving, B minus C the compile cache's. Their **difference**, (A minus B) minus (B minus C), ranks the caches only if its interval excludes zero; negative favours the compile cache.

concepts.term: Two clocks and the platform residual
concepts.plain: **Clock A** (laptop) brackets the whole job and sees it finish only when the laptop polls the job status, every 5 s; total [cold start](p1:coldstart) is its span minus the worker-clock warmup after the first request. **Clock B** (worker) starts just before `vllm serve`. **Platform time** = total minus clock B time, the one allowed cross-clock subtraction: handler start, teardown and up to one 5 s poll of lag. Clock C shows about 1 s of handler time outside clock B; container boot is not shown. RunPod's platform queue delay alone was about 0.13 s (median), so this is not queueing.
**p90** is the time 90% of runs finish within; p50 is the median. An **[ECDF](p2:ecdf)** plots every run (seconds across, share finished up), so the tail stays visible.

**H1**: weight handling is over half of worker-clock time through the first request in arm A. **H2**: volume weights cut it materially. **H3**: compiling is a non-trivial part of engine start, and a warm cache cuts it. **H4**: host differences drive how far p95 sits above the median. **H5**: a warm compile cache leaves more [KV cache](p1:kvcache). H1 holds only by its definition: weight handling is a median 0.58 of worker-clock time in arm A, above half in all 100 runs, but mostly server start-up; vLLM's own loading time is 17.40 s of 79.09 s, about 22%.

Hypotheses, contrasts, which runs to throw out, when to stop and how to pick the headline, committed in `docs/experiment.md` before any priming or campaign run (after three paid reconnaissance captures), four days before the first retained run; later changes are dated [amendments](p2:amendment) in git.

walkthrough.title: Where GPU memory goes, and what a warm compile cache buys
walkthrough.lead: Follow vLLM's memory budget through one start, from 21.64 GiB planned to tokens of KV cache, after a cold compile and then a warm one.

steps.say: The card reports 23.52 GiB of [GPU memory](p1:hbm). vLLM plans with 0.92 of it, a 21.64 GiB budget, and the [KV cache](p1:kvcache) gets whatever the other items leave.
Loading the [weights](p1:weights) takes 15.27 GiB. Counting vLLM's "non-torch" memory too, the log says 15.54 GiB used. That is the same in all 300 runs, whatever the arm.
On a cold compile cache the engine now runs [torch.compile](p1:compile), a median 18.79 s in arm B. The compile finishes before the profiling pass logs its numbers.
Then vLLM runs one profiling pass and records how high the activations peak. After a cold compile the log reports 1.18 GiB.
The KV cache is sized once, from what is left: 21.64 − 15.54 − 1.18 = 4.92 GiB. At 144 KiB per token the log counts 35,792 tokens. That size is fixed for the replica's life.
Arm C changes one thing from B: the compile cache is warm, so compile takes 0.33 s. The same profiling pass now reports 0.19 GiB of peak activation instead of 1.18.
Same subtraction, bigger remainder: 21.64 − 15.54 − 0.19 = 5.91 GiB. The log counts 43,040 tokens, room for 5 full-length requests. Every other term is unchanged.
The 0.99 GiB gained is exactly the 0.99 GiB the peak dropped. The log shows the drop, not its cause; [H5](a1:hypotheses) registered the compiler's memory still being resident during profiling.

walkthrough.takeaway: A warm compile cache saves seconds, and it lowers the peak the profiler measures. That leaves 0.99 GiB, or 7,248 tokens, more KV cache for as long as the replica lives.

decisions.title: Three arms, one variable
decisions.problem: Two caches start empty: the weights and the compiled code. To rank them, each comparison must change one thing only.
options: Two arms: hub vs volume weights
Add a baked-image arm, weights inside the container image
Add the fourth cell: weights cold, compile cache warm
One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.chosen: One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.why: A to B isolates the weight cache. B to C isolates the compile cache, weight handling held constant. The configuration is one frozen object that sets two paths, so the single-variable claim is true by structure. A baked image only moves the bytes into the image pull, inside the unsplit platform residual, flattering the weight time unseen. Nobody warms a compile cache while re-downloading weights, so the fourth cell answers no question.
decisions.cost: A warm arm needs a primed volume, and a test has to check that the arms differ nowhere else.
decisions.why_short: A to B isolates the weight cache, B to C the compile cache; one frozen configuration makes the single-variable claim true by structure.
decisions.cost_short: Arm C needs a primed volume, and a test checks that the arms differ nowhere else.

serves.because: One frozen configuration sets both cache paths, so each arm differs from the next in exactly one thing.

uses.because: Each cache gets its own one-step comparison: A to B, B to C.
Each adjacent pair of arms yields one contrast.

decisions.title: Measure from outside the engine
decisions.problem: vLLM's interesting phases are internal, and part of every cold start (queue, container start, image pull) happens before our code exists.
options: Time startup through vLLM's Python engine API
Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a worker clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.chosen: Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a worker clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.why: The Python API would measure a startup path nobody deploys. Two clocks make a lying clock detectable: the implemented check compares the laptop and worker clocks and discards a run whose total leaves no room for a network round trip.
decisions.cost: Platform time is one residual: handler start, teardown and up to one 5 s poll of lag. RunPod's own queue and execution durations (clock C) are recorded but not used to split it; its platform queue delay alone was about 0.13 s (median), so the residual is not queueing. Two engine sub-phases (device init and KV allocation) are not delineated by this vLLM build, so they sit merged in an unattributed row. The log patterns are tied to vLLM 0.27.1.
decisions.why_short: Timing the real `vllm serve` from outside measures the path people deploy, and a second clock lets a lying run be caught.
decisions.cost_short: Platform time is one residual (container start, teardown, poll lag), not queueing; two engine sub-phases stay merged.

serves.because: Engine phases come from vLLM's own log; what it cannot split goes in a labelled unattributed row and the platform residual, so nothing is hidden.

uses.because: Two clocks give platform time by subtraction and catch a run whose clocks disagree.

decisions.title: Interleave the arms in random triples
decisions.problem: Conditions on rented GPUs change over hours and days. Run the arms in blocks and a busy evening gets labelled as an arm effect.
options: Blocks: all of A, then all of B, then all of C
Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.chosen: Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.why: Blocking confounds the cache with time-of-day conditions, and on rented GPUs that confound can make or erase the whole effect. Triples also allow a paired, same-host check as supporting evidence.
decisions.cost: A resumed campaign must rebuild the exact schedule, so the harness refuses a resume whose stored arms disagree with the seed. The three windows (about 2 hours each, all on one host) fell on consecutive days, 19.8 and 17.5 hours apart, so some day-to-day drift is covered but longer-term drift is not.
decisions.why_short: Running all of one arm first would mix the cache effect with time-of-day conditions on the platform.
decisions.cost_short: A resume must rebuild the exact schedule; three ~2 h windows on consecutive days cover only some drift.

serves.because: In blocks, the time of day changes along with the arm, so a busy evening would pose as an arm effect.

uses.because: A triple puts all three arms in one stretch of time, so drift hits each alike.

decisions.title: Check each arm's cache state
decisions.problem: A warm cache leaking into a cold arm, or a cold compile inside arm C, would still produce plausible numbers. The configuration alone does not show what was on disk.
options: Let arm C's first campaign runs warm the cache
Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.chosen: Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.why: Without priming, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not: a mixture whose effect grows with run index, which looks like a real trend. So two priming runs go to a separate store, and the second must show the cache present and compile under one second. Cold paths are named by run id so a reused worker cannot hand one run's files to another. The cache state is checked before the engine starts, since a cold compile creates the directory as it finishes; a run whose state disagrees with its arm is discarded.
decisions.cost: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number. Checking after the engine run would look harmless but quietly discard about two thirds of a paid campaign, so the code carries a do-not-move warning.
decisions.why_short: Unprimed, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not, which looks like a real trend.
decisions.cost_short: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number.

serves.because: A leaked warm cache, or a cold compile in arm C, would make the arms differ in more than configuration, which alone does not show what was on disk.

uses.because: Each arm has an expected cache state, so a run whose observed state disagrees can be caught and discarded.

decisions.title: Rank the caches by the difference's interval
decisions.problem: Which cache buys more? Two effects, each with its own interval, do not answer that.
options: Subtract the weight-time contrast from the compile-time contrast
Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.chosen: Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.why: "Compile cache mattered more" is only a finding if the gap between the two effects excludes zero. The difference needs one shared unit, so it is computed on total cold start; subtracting weight time from compile time would difference two different quantities. The headline rule, lead with what transfers furthest to other infrastructure, was committed before the campaign data.
decisions.cost: Total time is read off the laptop's 5 s status poll, so each total carries up to one poll of lag (just above arm A's median the sorted totals jump 4.6 s), and the interval spans about three poll steps: −10.39 s, 95% [−20.30, −5.54]. The pre-registration requires it reported before any ranking claim. On the worker clock, which has no poll lag and leaves platform time out, the same difference is −12.16 s [−15.54, −10.74]: an exploratory check, not the pre-registered result.
decisions.why_short: "Compile cache mattered more" is a finding only if the gap between the two effects excludes zero.
decisions.cost_short: Total time carries up to one 5 s poll of lag, so the interval is wide; the ranking claim must always carry it.

serves.because: Two savings side by side do not rank the caches; only an interval on their difference can.
Leading with what transfers furthest, a rule committed before the campaign data, stops the headline being picked afterwards.

uses.because: The ranking is the difference of the two contrasts.
The pre-registration requires the difference's interval before any ranking claim.

decisions.title: Report the shape, and what it cannot answer
decisions.problem: Cold starts have a heavy right tail, and 100 runs per arm cannot support every summary.
options: Drop the host hypothesis (H4) quietly once every run lands on one host
p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.chosen: p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.why: A mean is pulled by the tail. At 100 runs a p99 is one or two observations, not an estimate. Before the published campaign began (a discarded window had already shown runs piling onto one host), the pre-registration committed to publishing the host count whatever it was. The same single host made every triple host-complete, so the paired check is fully supplied.
decisions.cost: The far tail stays unresolved: B's largest repeat-host runs were longer than A's. Two of B's three slowest also had slow weight loads (17.45 and 66.2 s against a 4.57 s median), and the slowest was the first run after a 19.8 h gap, so a cold host cache is one possible reading, unverified; if so, the 4.57 s volume load is a warm-host figure. Whether host placement drives the tail is unanswered.
decisions.why_short: A mean hides the tail, and at 100 runs a p99 would be one or two observations.
decisions.cost_short: The far tail stays unresolved, and whether host placement drives it is unanswered.
decisions.short: Report the shape and its limits

serves.because: A mean is pulled by the tail, so percentiles and the full ECDF describe real runs instead.
H4 was fixed in advance, so it is reported as unanswerable instead of quietly dropped.

uses.because: p50 to p95 hold up at 100 runs per arm.
H4 asked whether host placement drives the tail, and one host cannot answer it.

results.title: Where each arm's median cold start goes

deltas.text: Weight cache only: vLLM's load falls 17.40 → 4.57 s, start-up 28.19 → 25.28 s; compile stays near 19 s.
Compile cache only: compile falls 18.79 → 0.33 s; start-up before load also falls, 25.28 → 16.67 s (F2).

results.axis: Median seconds per phase, 100 runs per arm, in clock order. A: nothing cached; B: weights cached; C: both. Platform is drawn first but includes teardown and poll lag. Unattributed: engine start the log gives no duration for; the design attributes it to device init and KV allocation, plus about 2 s after graph capture. Its place here is not measured. Capture to first request: graph capture, the ready check (end of engine start until the health endpoint answers, polled every 0.25 s) and the first request (up to 16 tokens; time to first token is 0.042 s).
results.read_as: Start-up before load: each run's launch-to-loaded time minus vLLM's own reported load time (17.40, 4.57, 4.54 s). Dashed box on C: B's compile time.
results.takeaway: Each cache shrinks the phase it acts on; C also starts up sooner than B, which the design did not expect.
results.arithmetic: Each segment is one phase's median over 100 runs (the last adds three medians), and medians do not add: the bars sum to 82.25, 66.07 and 38.77 s against median totals of 81.12, 65.43 and 39.37 s.

results.title: Start-up and load, from the log
results.short: Start-up and load, from the log
results.axis: Median gaps between five log lines (four gaps), 100 runs per arm; 1 s timestamp resolution. About 6 s before the first line is not shown.
results.read_as: C's head start is the first gap (10 s in A and B, 1 s in C), in the API server before the engine core starts. Its cause is not confirmed; a cached model-inspection result is the working guess.
results.takeaway: C's head start precedes the engine core; its cause is unconfirmed.

results.title: How spread out the runs are

chart.note: Hollow circle: the arm's largest repeat-host run; the post gives it for A and B only.

results.axis: Seconds of total cold start per arm: p50 (median), p90, p95.
results.read_as: The arm order holds at every percentile shown; hollow markers show it break in the far tail. No p99: at 100 runs it would be one or two runs.
results.arithmetic: Percentiles use all 300 publishable runs, among them arm A's 2266.6 s run on a host's first image pull (far past p95) (hollow markers: A over 99 runs, B over 100).
results.takeaway: The ranking holds to p95; in the far tail, B's largest run exceeds A's.

results.title: Every run: the ECDF
results.axis: Share of each arm's repeat-host runs (99, 100, 100) finished by each total, in whole seconds and per cents; dashed lines: medians.
results.read_as: The curves climb in steps about 5 s apart, as the laptop's 5 s status poll would make them: arm A's totals ranked 41 to 51 lie at 80.92–81.16 s, ranks 52 to 61 at 85.72–85.89 s, none between, and 289 of 299 clock A spans fall within 0.25 s of one 5.175 s grid.
results.takeaway: The 5 s stairs are the poll grid.

results.title: Each effect on its own
results.axis: Seconds of total cold start each cache saves (median difference), with a 95% bootstrap interval.
results.read_as: Both clear zero, but side by side they do not rank the caches; the next chart does. Only 18.46 s of the compile cache's 26.07 s is compilation; the other 7.6 s roughly matches the 8.68 s start-up gap (F1). B − C is lopsided because B's runs ranked 41 to 56 lie at 65.35–65.80 s and rank 57 is 70.29 s: about one resample in ten lifts B's median into that cluster (70.4 − 39.4 = 31.0, the top), while the packed low runs leave the bottom 0.10 s under the estimate.
results.takeaway: Each cache saves time on its own, with neither interval near zero; context, not the ranking.
results.arithmetic: A − B and B − C use unrounded medians, so 15.68 and 26.07 s, not the 15.69 and 26.06 the rounded medians (81.12, 65.43, 39.37) give.

results.title: Which cache bought more
results.axis: Weight-cache saving minus compile-cache saving: seconds of total cold start, 95% bootstrap interval.
results.read_as: The whole interval, −20.30 to −5.54 s, lies left of zero, which licenses the ranking. It is a plausible range for the true difference, not where a re-run would land, and it is wide partly because each total carries up to one 5 s poll of lag (the ECDF shows the stairs); on the worker clock the same difference is −12.16 s [−15.54, −10.74], an exploratory check.
results.takeaway: The compile cache saves about 10 s more per cold start, and the interval never crosses zero: a finding, not a reading of two bars.
results.arithmetic: 15.68 − 26.07 = −10.39 s, on unrounded medians; the interval comes from 10,000 resamples of the runs.

results.title: KV cache left for serving, by arm
results.axis: KV cache tokens vLLM allocated at startup, same card and flags in every arm.
results.read_as: C keeps 20.3 % more KV cache. It shows up in the engine log's peak activation (1.18 GiB cold, 0.19 GiB warm); the subtraction is in How it works. Registered ahead as H5, though reconnaissance had logged both values once.
results.takeaway: B and C differ only in the compile cache, yet C gets 20.3 % more KV cache: one more full-length (8192-token) request at a time.
results.arithmetic: 43,040 / 8,192 = 5.25 and 35,792 / 8,192 = 4.37 full-length requests; the code keeps whole requests (rounds down), so 5 against 4. 43,040 / 35,792 = 1.203, so 20.3 % more.

interview.pitch30: I measured where the time goes when a vLLM server starts cold on a rented GPU, and which of two caches is worth warming: the model weights or the engine's compiled code. I ran three set-ups differing in one thing only, interleaved, a hundred times each, and split every start into phases. The compile cache saved about 10 seconds more per cold start than the weight cache, 95% interval 5.5 to 20 seconds more, and it left about 20% more KV cache for serving.
interview.pitch120: Everyone talks about caching the weights, but vLLM also compiles parts of the model at startup and caches that on disk. I set up three arms that differ only in cache configuration: nothing cached, weights on a network volume, and weights plus a warm compile cache. I ran them as shuffled triples so platform drift could not pose as an arm effect, and I committed my hypotheses and rules before any campaign data (after three reconnaissance captures). I timed the real `vllm serve` with one clock in the worker and one on my laptop, so platform start-up is a named residual, not hidden. The answer: warming the compile cache saved about 10 seconds more per cold start than caching the weights, and the interval on that difference never crossed zero. It also left about a fifth more KV cache; the registered explanation is that profiling no longer ran next to the compiler's memory, which the log fits but does not show. What it cannot tell you is anything about other hardware, or whether host placement drives the tail: every run landed on one machine, and I reported that rather than dropping the question.

followups.q: Why three arms and not two, or four?
followups.a: Two arms (hub vs volume) only test the weight cache: the fallback had this vLLM not compiled at startup; it does. A to B isolates weights, B to C compile with weights fixed. The fourth cell, weights cold but compile warm, has no operational meaning. A baked-image arm would only move the bytes into the image pull, which I cannot observe.

The git timestamp is the only evidence that the hypotheses and headline rule came before the campaign data; three paid reconnaissance captures came first and had already shown H5's two KV values once. Later amendments are dated: the first-touch rule, 32 minutes after window one showed a 2174 s platform time, and the H4 scoping after the discarded window. None changed a contrast or the headline rule; the H4 scoping narrowed a hypothesis.

C reached "model loaded" 8.85 s sooner than B, on arms differing only in compile cache, while vLLM's own model-loading time is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s): not host, not position in the triple. The engine log's own timestamps put almost all of the gap before the engine core starts, between the arguments line and architecture resolution: about 10 s in B, about 1 s in C. Arm C warms the whole vLLM cache directory, not just compiled code; my best guess is a cached model-inspection result there, which I have not confirmed. And "ready is not fast" was wrong here: [vLLM](p1:vllm) does its warmup before answering health, so the first request is already near steady state.

The host question failed: a serially-submitting driver kept landing on the one machine that had the image cached. The three windows ran on consecutive days, 19.8 and 17.5 hours apart, so drift over a longer period is not covered. And the first window was thrown out because arm A's per-run [weights](p1:weights) filled the worker disk (A failed 3 of its 9 runs, C one, B none), which would have biased the contrast; the worker now empties cold directories before and after each run.

followups.q: What does this not tell you?
followups.a: The seconds for any other GPU, model, engine version, region or provider. Anything about many [serverless](p1:serverless) replicas starting at once and contending for the same volume; every run was one replica alone. Anything past p95. And whether host placement drives the tail.

followups.q: So should everyone warm the compile cache?
followups.a: It is the better buy and the more fragile one. A [compile cache](p1:compile) costs nothing to store, but any change to engine version, model, hardware or flags invalidates it, so every upgrade pays the cold compile again unless warming is built into the deploy. The weight cache is a volume you rent every month whether you scale or not.

interview.limits: One provider, GPU model, model, engine version, region and host: the seconds do not transfer; the mechanisms may transfer, but only this setup was measured. H4 (does host placement drive the tail?) is unanswerable: all 300 runs landed on one host. Single replica, no contention. No percentile past p95. The first-touch rule that keeps the 2266.6 s run out of the ECDF (it stays in the medians) was written after seeing the data: post hoc.

recall.q: B and C differ only in the compile cache. Which chart segment should change, and which other one changed?
recall.a: Only compile should move, and it does: 18.79 to 0.33 s. The launch segment also shrank, 30.35 to 21.34 s, though vLLM's own loading time is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s). The engine log puts the gap before the engine core starts (about 10 s in B, 1 s in C); its cause is unconfirmed.

recall.q: On the one-run view, where does clock B start, and what lands in platform time?
recall.a: At step 4: the probe starts clock B just before launching `vllm serve`. Platform time is everything the laptop clock sees outside it: handler start before; teardown and up to one 5 s poll of lag after. RunPod's platform queue delay alone was only about 0.13 s.

recall.q: Why is arm C primed outside the campaign?
recall.a: Otherwise its early runs compile cold and its later runs do not, making the arm a mixture whose effect grows with run index and looks like a trend.

recall.q: Why is the compile cache checked before the engine starts, not after?
recall.a: A cold compile creates the cache directory as it finishes. Checked afterwards, every healthy cold run would look warm and be discarded, and a cold compile inside arm C would pass as warm.

recall.q: How is a contrast obtained, and why does the ranking need a third number?
recall.a: Subtract the medians of two arms that differ in one cache, with a bootstrap interval. Which cache saves more is a claim about the difference of the two contrasts, so it needs its own interval, on one shared unit: total cold start.

recall.q: If the difference's interval had run from −20 to +3 s, what could you claim?
recall.a: Not the ranking, which needs the interval to exclude zero: no difference, or a slightly larger weight-cache saving, would still fit. Each cache's own saving could still be reported.

recall.q: Which requirement breaks if the arms run in blocks, and what protects it?
recall.a: R2, one change per comparison: in blocks, time-of-day platform conditions change along with the cache. Interleaved triples protect it, with one frozen cache configuration and the per-run check of each arm's compile-cache state.

recall.q: Why is a failed run never retried in place?
recall.a: A retry quietly swaps slow or unlucky runs for faster ones, flattering the distribution. Failures are their own rows, counted per arm.

recall.q: Why does the warm compile cache leave more KV cache?
recall.a: The KV cache is sized from what is left after the weights and the profiling pass's peak. A cold compile gives a higher peak (1.18 vs 0.19 GiB), so less is left. The registered cause (H5): the compiler's memory is still resident during profiling.
